newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ulster Bank 1996 profit 136 mln stg.
newsitem.headline: Ulster Bank 1996 profit 136 mln stg.

text.p: Ulster Bank, a wholly-owned subsidiary of NatWest Plc, reported a 1996 pretax profit of 136 million sterling in the year to Dec 31, 1996 against a 1995 profit of 120 million.
Operating income rose by 33 million pounds, a 10 per cent increase, to 350 million pounds.
Net interest income was up 17 million, an eight per cent rise, to 229 million, the bank said in a results statement.
Provision for bad and doubtful debts rose three million pounds to eight million due to an increase in the general provision.
The bank said its 1996 profits were the highest ever.
Non-interest income was up by 15 percent by 16 million sterling to 121 million largely due to increased fees and services business.

Ulster Bank Retail, which includes the core branch network, mortgage, instalment credit, leasing and invoice discounting operations, increased profits 17 percent to 81 million pounds largely due to lending growth.

Ulster Bank Markets, the corporate banking, treasury, investment management and stockbroking business, contributed an increased pretax profit of 55 million pounds, an eight percent increase of four million pounds.
Kells said in a results statement that every one of the group's operations had improved on its 1995 performance and that its 1996 profits were the highest ever.
Ulster reported a 1996 pretax profit of 136 million sterling in the year to Dec 31, 1996, against a 1995 profit of 120 million.

Lending was up 13 per cent or 474 million sterling to 4,130 million,operating income rose by 33 million pounds, a 10 per cent rise, to 350 million while net interest income was up 17 million, an eight per cent rise, to 229 million.

"Loans and advances to customer rose by 13 per cent and, despite the competitive pressure on margins, growth in business volumes yielded an increase in net interest income of eight per cent," Kells said.
Kells said that growth had been achieved across a wide portfolio of operations in Ulster Bank Retail.
"Branch profitability improved principally as a result of good growth in lending, current accounts, and deposits. An additional 100 staff were recruited into our retail business in 1996," he said.

Ulster said there was strong economic growth, both North and South in Ireland and, as a result of its attention to the customer, it had not only increased its range of services to existing customers but had expanded its customer base throughout the island.
It said it was committed to strong, continued growth across the island.

"The whole island has the economic ball at its toe and the bank is unreservedly committed to helping it kick the ball into the net. For Northern Ireland in particular, peace and stability can release very significant economic potential," Sir George Quigley, Ulster Bank Chairman, said.

"There are excellent foundations on which to build, as demonstrated by the existing levels of local and inward investment, the sharp decline in unemployment and a buoyant housing market with house prices up 12 per cent during the year," he added.
He said the recent rapid expansion in trade between both parts of the island held out the promise of increasingly strong and mutually advantageous business links.

"Since Ulster Bank does almost all its business within the island, our fortunes are inextricably linked with its prosperity. It is here that we reinvest our profits and expand employment," Quigley said.
Ulster said the opportunity to purchase Ireland's TSB Bank was still one important option for expansion, provided it can be acquired on terms which make good commercial sense.
